quote: Was entspricht also [-in der Arithmetik-] den ganzen [-Z-] Zahlen in der [-x-] Analysis, die auch so ein ganzes Gebäude aufzurichten, sobald man ihre Festsetzungen[?] der Anschau- ung entnommen hat?
english: What, then, corresponds to the integers in analysis, which likewise allow a whole edifice to be erected once one has taken their stipulations from intuition?
topic: Hilbert notes lecture plans (reading elliptic functions following Liouville, and a course on pure geometry with axioms, Euclidean geometry, analysis situs and projective geometry), a plan to study when two solutions of his discriminant problem coincide, and a remark that an irrational number contains nothing infinite.

triage.modern_statement: This is a foundational, programmatic question rather than a single theorem. In modern terms: for analysis, what basic system plays the part the integers play in arithmetic? That is, what can be laid down as a small set of axioms taken from intuition, from which all of analysis can then be built? Read this way, the question asks for an axiomatic characterization of the real number continuum. The usual answer today is the axioms of a complete ordered (Archimedean) field. Behind it sits a second question: are those axioms consistent?
triage.answered_by: Hilbert himself took this up in public soon after. In 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (Jahresbericht DMV, 1900; talk given in 1899) he set out axioms for the real numbers: field and order axioms, the Archimedean axiom and an axiom of completeness. These characterize the reals as a complete ordered field. At the Paris ICM in 1900 he then made the consistency of these 'arithmetical axioms' (axioms for analysis) his 2nd Problem. That consistency question is the part still unresolved. Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) showed it cannot be settled in the finitary way Hilbert hoped. Consistency proofs using stronger methods came later, for example Gentzen's 1936 proof for arithmetic of the natural numbers; no comparable proof exists yet for full analysis (the theory of the reals).

evidence.claim: Hilbert put forward axioms for the real numbers, including an axiom of completeness, in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900).
The arithmetical axioms in Hilbert's 2nd problem really concern analysis, i.e. the theory of complete ordered fields. Hilbert pointed to 'Über den Zahlbegriff' for how they are formulated.
Hilbert's 2nd problem asks for the compatibility (consistency) of the arithmetical axioms and was the starting point of his program for the foundations of mathematics.
The 2nd problem asked for a proof that the arithmetic axioms are consistent. Because of Gödel's work it is regarded as partly resolved in the negative.

triage.why: The note asks what in analysis corresponds to the integers in arithmetic: a basic system whose stipulations are taken from intuition and on which a whole theory can be built. That is the axiomatization of the reals that Hilbert published in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900), and he made the consistency of those axioms his 2nd Paris problem. The sources do not tie this particular notebook entry to the 1900 paper, so the link is a reading of the content, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. The axiomatization part was answered by Hilbert himself. The consistency part was changed fundamentally by Gödel. The consistency strength of analysis and its subsystems is still actively studied today, in proof theory and in reverse mathematics; that last point is my general knowledge and is not among the cited sources.
